title: Receivables outgrowing sales
text: When receivables grow much faster than sales, revenue may be booked before cash is collectible: bill-and-hold, extended payment terms, or sales to customers who cannot pay. Compare the change in receivables with the change in sales and check whether days sales outstanding jumped in the year under review.

title: Sales growth without cash sales growth
text: Reported sales that rise while cash collected from customers (sales minus the increase in receivables) is flat or falling suggest accrual-driven revenue. A large gap between change in sales and change in cash sales is a classic early warning of premature or fictitious revenue.

title: Year-end revenue push
text: Companies under pressure to meet targets may pull next-period sales into the current year. Signs in annual numbers: a spike in receivables at year end, unusually strong final-year growth versus prior years, and a margin improvement that later reverses.

title: Growth that breaks the firm's own trend
text: A sudden acceleration in sales growth that is far outside the firm's own multi-year history deserves explanation. Look at two to four prior years: a firm that grew 3 percent a year and suddenly reports 40 percent growth without acquisitions or new financing warrants scrutiny.

title: Capitalizing operating costs
text: Moving ordinary operating costs onto the balance sheet raises earnings and assets at the same time. Watch for gross PP&E or other assets rising faster than sales, falling expense ratios, and soft assets growing as a share of total assets.

title: Slowing depreciation
text: Extending useful lives or changing depreciation methods lowers depreciation expense. A falling depreciation rate (depreciation divided by gross PP&E) relative to prior years, a depreciation index above one, or depreciation shrinking while PP&E grows, can indicate income-boosting choices.

title: Margin improvement too good to be true
text: A gross margin that improves sharply while sales growth also accelerates, and without a clear cost driver, may reflect understated cost of goods sold, for example by overstating ending inventory. Check margin change against inventory build-up.

title: Inventory build-up
text: Inventory rising faster than sales or cost of goods sold may signal overstated inventory, which simultaneously understates cost of goods sold and inflates profit. It may also mean obsolete stock that should have been written down.

title: Soft assets share
text: Soft assets are total assets minus cash and net PP&E. A high or rising share of soft assets gives managers more room for judgment in valuation, and research links it to a higher likelihood of misstatement.

title: Other investments and advances
text: Growth in other investments, advances or miscellaneous assets can hide related-party transactions or round-tripping of cash. Large unexplained increases in these lines, particularly in a year of strong reported earnings, deserve follow-up.

title: Earnings far above cash flow
text: When income is high but operating cash flow is weak, profits rest on accruals rather than cash. Large positive working-capital or total accruals relative to assets are among the most reliable statistical predictors of later restatement.

title: Change in total accruals
text: An increase in accruals from one year to the next (for example the RSST accrual measure) is more informative than the level. A sharp jump in accruals in the year under review suggests earnings management that year.

title: Working-capital accruals
text: Growth in non-cash current assets net of current liabilities (excluding cash and short-term debt) raises reported income without cash. Large increases in receivables and inventory with flat payables drive this signal.

title: Falling free cash flow with rising earnings
text: Free cash flow that declines while net income rises is a divergence that often precedes restatements. It can reflect aggressive revenue recognition, capitalized costs, or working-capital manipulation.

title: Cash-flow classification
text: Operating cash flow can be flattered by moving operating outflows into investing activities or by classifying financing inflows as operating. Compare operating cash flow with earnings and with capital spending trends across several years.

title: Capital-raising pressure
text: Firms that issue debt or equity in the year under review, or plan to, have incentives to look strong. Misstatement is more common in years with securities issuance, especially when combined with high accruals.

title: Leverage and covenant pressure
text: Rising debt, current debt coming due, and thin interest coverage create pressure to avoid covenant breaches. Combined with improving reported earnings and weak cash flow, this pattern is a risk signal.

title: High valuation expectations
text: A low book-to-market ratio (a high market valuation relative to book equity) means the market expects growth. Managers may misstate to meet those expectations, especially after a run of reported growth.

title: Improving ROA under pressure
text: A rise in return on assets after a period of decline, without a change in strategy or industry conditions, can come from income-increasing accruals. Check whether the improvement is backed by cash.

title: Cash margin deterioration
text: Cash margin is cash sales minus cash costs, divided by cash sales. A declining cash margin while reported profit margins hold steady points to accrual-based profit.

title: Understated liabilities
text: Accounts payable, accrued liabilities or taxes payable that fall while activity grows may indicate unrecorded expenses or liabilities. Compare the trend in current liabilities with cost of goods sold and sales.

title: Tax expense and pretax income mismatch
text: Income tax expense that is very low relative to reported income, or taxes payable that do not move with earnings, may mean book income is overstated relative to taxable income.

title: Retained earnings versus reported profits
text: Retained earnings that do not grow consistently with reported net income and dividends can reveal adjustments recorded directly to equity or prior misstatements. A low retained-earnings-to-assets ratio also signals a young or struggling firm.

title: Declining fundamentals masked by growth
text: Firms whose underlying performance is deteriorating, such as falling ROA or shrinking cash sales, have stronger incentives to misstate. Fraud often begins after a period of genuine decline.

title: Diagnostic versus confirmatory checks
text: A good analyst tests the strongest explanation against evidence that could refute it. Rather than confirming that growth looks healthy, check whether cash, receivables and inventory support the growth. Rather than assuming fraud, check whether a benign business reason fits all the numbers.

title: Benign explanations
text: Not every anomaly is manipulation. Acquisitions, rapid organic expansion, seasonality, new product launches and industry cycles can all move receivables, inventory and accruals. A red flag is stronger when several independent signals point the same way.

title: Base rates
text: Material misstatement is rare: well under 1 in 100 public company-years are later subject to SEC enforcement. Even strong signals produce many false positives, so risk scores should reflect how unusual a firm is compared with peers, not just whether a ratio moved.

title: Short-term investments and cash
text: Reported cash and short-term investments that are large relative to operations yet do not generate interest income, or that appear alongside heavy borrowing, may be overstated or restricted.

title: Interest expense versus debt
text: Interest expense that is low relative to average debt may indicate capitalized interest or unrecorded borrowing costs. Compare interest expense with debt balances over several years.

title: Multi-year pattern of accrual reversal
text: Accrual manipulation must eventually reverse. A history of high accruals followed by a sudden write-down, or several years of steadily rising accruals, helps distinguish persistent manipulation from one-off timing effects.
